1:
The psalm has no title and no fixable date. Clarke says neither occasion nor author can be determined, and reports that fifteen manuscripts run the two together as one. Delitzsch agrees, notes that the Greek ascribed it to David without warrant, and explains its position: it stands here only because its last verse accords with the last verse but one of the psalm before. The Jewish sources group it with another as a protective song for times of danger. Augustine frames the whole poem by one episode, this being the psalm from which the devil dared to tempt Christ. Let us attend to it, he says, that so armed we may resist the tempter — not presuming in ourselves but in him who was tempted first, whose answers to the devil are the answers we are to give.

What the opening promises, and to whom, is where they separate. Spurgeon restricts it: these blessings are not for all believers but for those who live in close fellowship with God. Every child of God looks toward the inner sanctuary, yet all do not dwell in the most holy place; they run to it at times without habitually residing there. Henry lays it down generally, that all who live in communion with God are safe under his protection: the true believer is at home in God and has not merely admittance but residence. Gill identifies the secret place with God's own heart, into which he takes his people. Calvin turns it into a rebuke: many talk of providence and profess that God guards his children, but few are willing to entrust their safety to him. He settles a construction: some read the first three verses as one sentence, since the first otherwise repeats itself, but he calls that forced — the clauses state distinct ideas, that no hostile weapon reaches the man hidden under divine protection, and that those who dwell there learn how far it reaches.

Who is speaking is disputed too. Gill takes the second verse for the psalmist's own words, though the Greek, Latin and Oriental versions make it the man in the secret place who says them. Clarke reports a tradition turning the psalm into a dialogue: David asserts the first verse, Solomon answers, David replies with the promises, God speaks the last three. Henry hears one voice and gives it an edge: I will say of the Lord whatever others say of him. Wesley reduces the condition to a clause: he that makes God his habitation and refuge.

The snare and the pestilence are read at several levels. Delitzsch takes the fowler for death, or him that has the power of death; Ellicott agrees the image covers any unexpected peril, and renders the second phrase as a pestilence of calamities. Clarke points out that the same Hebrew letters give both a word spoken and a pestilence, so some render deliverance from the slanderous word and others from the disease. Gill runs through the candidates for the fowler — Saul, any persecutor, or best of all Satan — while Wesley keeps it to the plague, which takes men suddenly. Spurgeon makes the widest application and guards it: there is a pestilence of error, of sin and of disease, and faith by cheering the heart keeps it free from the fear that in a plague kills more than the plague — though he admits it does not always ward off death. On the covering wings, Clarke recalls the Greek reading, he will overshadow thee between his shoulders, alluding to parents carrying weak children on their backs, and takes the truth that shields to be God's revelation. Delitzsch hears the older passage about the eagle's wing behind it, and takes the rare word beside shield for a weapon surrounding the body. Gill keeps the tenderness: birds cover young that cannot cover themselves, the condition of the children of God.
5:
The four perils are read as figures, as facts, and occasionally as demons. Clarke observes that night is a time of terrors because it is a time of treasons, plunder and murder, while the godly man sleeps quietly. He records the Chaldee, which turns the verse into a warning against the demons that walk by night, and reports that the rabbins supposed death's empire divided between two demons, one ruling by day and one by night — the Latin and Greek even naming the noonday destroyer. Ellicott keeps to climate and idiom: night and noon are the unwholesome hours in the East, the one from exhalations and the other from heat, and the word for destruction means by parallelism a deadly sickness. He allows the night terror to be an enemy attack, in which case the arrow would be battle, but thinks it may equally be the Eastern name for the plague, which Arabians still call God's arrow.

Gill takes the second verse as explaining the first, and draws the plague itself: the name of it at a distance is terrible and its approach more so, and by night it is worse than by day — not only to think of in the gloomy watches, but to see the numbers carried out and hear the cry, bring out your dead. Wesley keeps the terms general: by night, when evil accidents are most terrible and least avoidable, and invisibly, which we neither foresee nor prevent. On the thousands falling, Gill insists the reference is not to battle but to the pestilence just described; Clarke reports a rendering that makes them enemies instead, falling upon the man on either side without coming near enough to take his life. Ellicott states the promise widely: the pronoun covers no one of the dangers enumerated, and the pious Israelite bears a charmed life, seeing only the effect of perils that pass him by.

The ninth verse has a change of person that nobody finds easy. Ellicott says the Authorised Version avoids the difficulty only by violence to the text, which runs literally, for thou, Jehovah, my refuge; thou hast made the Most High thy habitation. He proposes reading the first line as a kind of under-soliloquy: the poet, assuring himself of the protection given to one who trusts God, breaks off to comment that this is true of himself. Gill reaches nearly the same result from the accents, which require because thou, Lord, art my refuge, leaving open whether the words are the good man's or the psalmist's. Delitzsch notes that the first voice continues the ratification, the promises rising ever higher. Henry and Clarke read it straight through as addressed to the man, who has taken the Most High for his portion, so that no evil shall come near his dwelling. Henry then draws out the character described — those who make God their habitation and his name both their temple and their strong tower. It is our duty to be at home in God, and afterwards our privilege, welcome as a man to his own house, without hindrance from the arrests of the law.

Spurgeon leaves exposition at this verse and tells what happened to him. In 1854, scarcely a year into his London ministry, cholera came to the neighbourhood where he worked. Family after family summoned him to the bedside of the smitten, and almost every day he was called to a grave; he gave himself to the visiting and grew weary and sick at heart. His friends seemed to be falling one by one, and he felt, or fancied, that he was sickening like those around him — a little more work and weeping would have laid him low. Returning from a funeral, he stopped at a paper pasted up in a shoemaker's window. It was no trade announcement but this verse, in a good bold hand.
10:
The promise that no evil shall befall is at once qualified. Gill points out that sin cleaves to the best of saints and afflictions come as chastisements; what never touches them is the evil of punishment, so that a public calamity falling on them with everyone else is not punishment and works for their good. Ellicott notes that the word for dwelling is literally a tent — patriarchal life fossilised in the language.

On the angels the readers agree in what they deny. Spurgeon says the verse gives not one guardian angel but all of them: the bodyguard of the princes of the blood imperial of heaven, charged to take special note of those who dwell in God. Ellicott makes the same denial historically: the notion of a personal guardian angel may have been encouraged by this verse but originated in heathen belief, and what the psalm charges them with is the care of all who fulfil the conditions laid down before. Clarke turns the point into a caution about worship: since God gives the angels charge, they are not to be prayed to nor praised, but God only. Their work he describes as turning a man's steps out of the way of danger and suggesting prudent counsels.

Whether the protection is conditional divides them by a hair. Clarke states it as a rule: the path of duty is the way of safety, and no man can expect protection who does not walk in obedience. Spurgeon reads the same clause as no restriction to a heart right with God, since it is not the believer's way to go out of his way: he keeps in the way, and then the angels keep him. Gill raises a different question. Satan applied the verse to Christ, and our Lord did not object; it can hardly be supposed the tempter would have ventured on it had the application been open to challenge — what he is to be blamed for is the purpose he quoted it for, and for leaving out the following clause, which he saw was against his design. On the bearing up in the hands, Clarke and Ellicott both picture a nurse carrying a child; Gill sees the helplessness of God's people, borne up through life and carried at death into Abraham's bosom.

The lion and the adder are read on three levels. Gill takes them first literally, of men delivered from savage creatures, then figuratively of Satan, called a lion for cruelty and a serpent for craft. Ellicott makes them emblems of the dangers that threaten life; Wesley extends the last to all pernicious creatures and all sorts of enemies. Clarke goes to natural history: the asp is a small serpent peculiar to Egypt and Libya, its poison killing without remedy and, it is said, painlessly — probably why an Egyptian queen chose it rather than grace a triumph. The word rendered dragon, he adds, often means any large aquatic animal.

At the close God speaks, as Wesley and Gill both note. Gill reads the love set on God as sincere, singular in being placed on him alone, and fixed; Ellicott renders it more simply as clung to me. Spurgeon presses the ground of the promise: not that the man deserves keeping, but that with all his imperfections he does love his God. Clarke notes that the assurance of presence is literally I am with him — as soon as the trouble comes he is there. On the long life, Gill observes that the saints live here as long as they choose and die full of years. Clarke renders it as filling a man with length of days — he shall neither live a useless life nor die before his time. Ellicott closes on its fitness: the promise of long life is peculiarly appropriate at the end of a psalm that has spoken throughout of dangers to life.
